clinician.final_diagnosis: ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema with concomitant COVID-19 infection
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 57-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes presented to the emergency department with acute onset tongue swelling, dysphonia, and dyspnea. He had been taking benazepril for 4 months. The angioedema was refractory to multiple doses of intramuscular epinephrine in the prehospital setting. Physical examination revealed pronounced lingual and perioral edema without pain, pruritus, or urticaria, with oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. In the emergency department, he received tranexamic acid with clinical improvement over 3 hours, along with intravenous diphenhydramine and famotidine; benazepril was withheld. He was admitted for airway monitoring. C1 esterase inhibitor testing was not reported. Soon after discharge, his COVID-19 PCR result returned positive, confirming concomitant infection.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Acute onset tongue swelling, dysphonia, and dyspnea refractory to epinephrine suggesting bradykinin-mediated mechanism
ACE inhibitor (benazepril) use for 4 months prior to presentation
Physical examination showing pronounced lingual and perioral edema without pain or pruritus (non-histaminergic features)
Clinical improvement over 3 hours following tranexamic acid administration with withholding of benazepril
Concomitant COVID-19 infection confirmed by positive PCR
Absence of urticaria, pruritus, or allergic triggers making histamine-mediated angioedema less likely

Absence of urticaria and pruritus; lack of response to epinephrine
